Using bayesfoRest with brms

Source: vignettes/brms.qmd

brms is the most fully-featured backend in bayesfoRest. Every plotting function works with a brmsfit, including the ones that need to refit the model: subgroup analyses and prior sensitivity (sensitivity_plot(), ecdf_model_plot(), ecdf_prior_plot()). If you’re not sure which backend to start with, start with brms.

Fit the model

bayesfoRest expects a two-column effect-and-standard-error outcome, fit with brms::brm(). Prepare the effect sizes with metafor::escalc() first:

library(metafor)
library(brms)
library(bayesfoRest)

binary_es <- escalc(
  measure = "OR",
  ai = Event_Intervention, bi = Outcome_Intervention_No,
  ci = Event_Control, di = Outcome_Control_No,
  n1i = N_Intervention, n2i = N_Control,
  data = binary_outcome) |>
  dplyr::mutate(sei = sqrt(vi))

A random-effect (hierarchical) model includes (1 | Author); a common-effect model drops it:

# Random-effect
model_re <- brm(
  yi | se(sei) ~ 1 + (1 | Author),
  family = gaussian(),
  data = binary_es,
  prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept) +
          prior(cauchy(0, 0.5), class = sd),
  iter = 4000,
  cores = parallel::detectCores(),
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  silent = 2)

# Common-effect
model_ce <- brm(
  yi | se(sei) ~ 1,
  family = gaussian(),
  data = binary_es,
  prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept),
  iter = 4000,
  cores = parallel::detectCores(),
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99),
  silent = 2)

bayes_forest() (and every other bayesfoRest function) auto-detects the pooling type from the model by checking for a sd_ draw – you don’t need to pass model_type unless you want to override it. See vignette("bayesfoRest") for the full forest plot walkthrough; this vignette focuses on what’s brms-specific.

Subgroup analysis

With subgroup = TRUE, bayesfoRest needs a per-subgroup pooled estimate. For brms it gets one automatically: refit_for_subgroup.brmsfit() calls stats::update(model, newdata = <subgroup rows>, recompile = FALSE) for each subgroup, reusing the compiled Stan model so this stays fast.

bayes_forest(
  model = model_re,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  n_ctrl = N_Control,
  n_int = N_Intervention,
  event_ctrl = Event_Control,
  event_int = Event_Intervention,
  subgroup = TRUE,
  subgroupvar = Subgroup,
  xlim = c(0.1, 3.5)
)

Backends without a refit_for_subgroup() method fall back to approximating subgroup effects from the overall model, with a warning. brms (along with bayesmeta, MetaStan, rstanarm and bayesma) refits properly.

Overall and funnel plots 

overall_plot(
  model = model_re,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  add_tau = TRUE,
  add_pred = TRUE,
  incl_mu_prior = TRUE,
  incl_tau_prior = TRUE
)

incl_mu_prior/incl_tau_prior read the priors directly from the brms fit (via brms::prior_summary()) and draw them on the same density scale as the posteriors – no need to re-specify them. This is currently only automatic for brms and bayesmeta; other backends need mu_prior/tau_prior passed in explicitly (e.g. mu_prior = bf_normal(0, 1)).

funnel_plot(
  model = model_re,
  data = binary_es,
  measure = "OR",
  studyvar = Author,
  yearvar = Year,
  yi_col = "yi",
  sei_col = "sei"
)

Prior sensitivity

brms can fit every prior family bf_*() offers – bf_normal(), bf_student_t(), bf_half_normal(), bf_half_cauchy(), bf_half_t(), bf_exponential(), bf_lognormal(), bf_uniform(), and the empirical bf_turner()/bf_rhodes() priors – so sensitivity_plot(), ecdf_model_plot() and ecdf_prior_plot() all work without restriction. Write the priors you want to compare with the bf_*() helpers:

priors <- list(
  vague = list(
    name      = "Vague",
    mu_prior  = bf_normal(0, 10),
    tau_prior = bf_half_cauchy(0, 1)),
  weakreg = list(
    name      = "Weakly Regularising",
    mu_prior  = bf_normal(0, 1),
    tau_prior = bf_half_cauchy(0, 0.5)),
  informative = list(
    name      = "Informative",
    mu_prior  = bf_normal(0, 0.5),
    tau_prior = bf_half_cauchy(0, 0.3))
)

sensitivity_plot() refits model_re under each prior and draws the pooled effect from every section you ask for. incl_random_effect (default TRUE) keeps the original random-effect sections; incl_common_effect = TRUE adds a common-effect refit for the same priors; exclude_high_rob = TRUE adds a section excluding studies with a high overall risk of bias (needs rob_var):

sensitivity_plot(
  model = model_re,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors,
  measure = "OR",
  rob_var = Overall,
  incl_random_effect = TRUE,
  incl_common_effect = TRUE,
  exclude_high_rob = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5)
)

ecdf_model_plot() fixes one prior and compares strategies (sections); ecdf_prior_plot() fixes one section and compares priors:

ecdf_model_plot(
  model = model_re,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors["weakreg"],
  measure = "OR",
  rob_var = Overall,
  incl_common_effect = TRUE,
  exclude_high_rob = TRUE,
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5)
)

ecdf_prior_plot(
  model = model_re,
  data = binary_es,
  priors = priors,
  measure = "OR",
  xlim = c(0.25, 1.5)
)

See vignette("sensitivity-analysis") for publication-bias-adjusted sensitivity sections built from a RoBMA fit (incl_robma, incl_pet_peese, incl_selection_weight).
